claim: Genetically encoded fluorescent glutamate indicators (iGluSnFRs) enable neurotransmitter release and diffusion to be visualized in intact tissue.
source: Genetically encoded fluorescent glutamate indicators (iGluSnFRs) enable neurotransmitter release and diffusion to be visualized in intact tissue.
evidence: This is a general statement about the capabilities of iGluSnFRs, supported by established knowledge in the field and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic iGluSnFR signal time courses vary widely depending on experimental conditions, often lasting 10–100 times longer than the extracellular lifetime of synaptically released glutamate estimated with uptake measurements.
source: Synaptic iGluSnFR signal time courses vary widely depending on experimental conditions, often lasting 10–100 times longer than the extracellular lifetime of synaptically released glutamate estimated with uptake measurements.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of published data on iGluSnFR signals and uptake measurements, as referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: iGluSnFR signals typically decay much more slowly than the unbinding kinetics of the indicator.
source: iGluSnFR signals typically also decay much more slowly than the unbinding kinetics of the indicator.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of measured decay kinetics with unbinding rates, as shown in the simulations and experiments.

claim: Simulations suggested that iGluSnFR competes with transporters to bind synaptically released glutamate, delaying glutamate uptake.
source: Simulations suggested that iGluSnFR competes with transporters to bind synaptically released glutamate, delaying glutamate uptake.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the Monte Carlo simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Synaptic transporter currents recorded from iGluSnFR-expressing astrocytes in mouse cortex were slower than those in control astrocytes.
source: Accordingly, synaptic transporter currents recorded from iGluSnFR-expressing astrocytes in mouse cortex were slower than those in control astrocytes.
evidence: This is supported by direct experimental measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: Simulations suggested that iGluSnFR reduces free glutamate levels in extrasynaptic spaces, likely limiting extrasynaptic receptor activation.
source: Simulations also suggested that iGluSnFR reduces free glutamate levels in extrasynaptic spaces, likely limiting extrasynaptic receptor activation.
evidence: This is supported by simulation results showing reduced glutamate concentrations in extrasynaptic regions.

claim: iGluSnFR and lower affinity variants provide linear indications of vesicle release.
source: iGluSnFR and lower affinity variants, nonetheless, provide linear indications of vesicle release, underscoring their value for optical quantal analysis.
evidence: This is supported by multi-synapse simulation results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Periplasmic binding proteins (PBPs) have been modified to develop genetically encoded biosensors to detect different molecules, including glutamate.
source: Periplasmic binding proteins (PBPs) have been modified to develop genetically encoded biosensors to detect different molecules, including glutamate (de Lorimier et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to de Lorimier et al., 2002.

claim: PBPs comprise two domains linked by flexible 'hinge' where ligand binding brings the two domains closer together.
source: PBPs comprise two domains linked by flexible 'hinge' where ligand binding brings the two domains closer together (Quiocho et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Quiocho et al., 1997.

claim: PBP glutamate indicators are based on GltI, part of E. Coli.'s ABC glutamate/aspartate transporter complex.
source: PBP glutamate indicators are based on GltI, part of E. Coli.'s ABC glutamate/aspartate transporter complex
evidence: This is established knowledge about the molecular basis of these indicators.
